extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and early-career journalists (cub reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters on preparing for and conducting interviews, taking and using notes, selecting quotations, judging information, handling different interviewee types, and organizing material for clear, accurate, and speedy news writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation: Learn the subject's history before interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reporter will take the trouble to learn the history of a person before he approaches him for a story, he will provide himself with the live talking points which are almost indispensable to his success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the interviewee's background and accomplishments before approaching them; intelligent interest warms even modest subjects and yields more substantive material. Failure to do so can derail an interview (example: reporter who didn't know the honoree and gained little usable material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger in Carelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting preparation can result in embarrassment and poor reporting — the reporter must know who the subject is and why an event occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overconfidence; prepare specifically (who, why). A pleasant manner cannot compensate for ignorance of key facts. Material obtained after careless approach tends to be weak and unusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding of Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the topic under discussion (e.g., music, baseball) is essential to ask intelligent questions and understand technical terms used by the interviewee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn fundamental facts about the subject before the interview. If unfamiliar, spend time studying basic terms and conventions so you can follow and probe effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility an Asset
rubrics_metrics.description: On small papers a reporter must cover a wide variety of assignments; to know a little about everything and a great deal about a few things should be the beginner's ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate broad general knowledge plus depth in some areas. When assigned an unfamiliar topic, do preparatory work beforehand even if irksome — it yields better interviews and stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reliance Best
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should not ask editors for details they can look up themselves; self-reliance and willingness to work hard are prized traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do your own legwork rather than relying on busy editors. Be unsparing of effort to ensure accuracy and interest in the story; laziness harms your reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality and Appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasing personality and attractive (neat, quiet) appearance help gain audience and confidence; avoid effrontery or overfamiliarity and maintain dignity representing the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be neither servile nor patronizing; use unassuming courtesy, pleasant smile, listen more than speak. Dress neatly; attend to nails, teeth, hair. Beware of using personal charms or flirting — intimacy often hinders rather than helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a Card
rubrics_metrics.description: A neatly engraved card with the reporter's name and paper can gain access, but sending a card where inappropriate is a blunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from experience when to use a card. With persons distrustful of newspapers, do not reveal purpose of call until you have obtained information. Choose approach to fit the interviewee and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Right Way to Ask Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Have most questions in mind before the interview but avoid a slavish, prearranged sequence; direct conversation by occasional remarks and avoid interrupting the flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare mentally but be flexible; let conversation flow and only steer occasionally. Never interrupt to ask trivial or irrelevant questions; get all needed information but drop surplus material later in organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Notebook and Pencil
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaching with pad and pencil in hand can make interviewees cautious; use judgment whether to take notes visibly or rely on other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size up the person and circumstances. Some will dictate or write answers; for 'ticklish' stories get signed statements and check them thoroughly. When notebook would inhibit conversation, rely on memory or discreet note-taking, then verify facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asking negative-form questions (e.g., 'You haven't any news today, have you?') because they invite discouraging answers and shape the respondent's reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase questions to stimulate thought and invite positive information ('What news have you for me today?'). The form and tone of the question affect responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of News
rubrics_metrics.description: The interviewer must be quick to perceive hints or chance remarks that open big stories, but may need to conceal that perception with reluctant talkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow up leads openly with willing interviewees; with reluctant ones proceed cautiously and avoid revealing you detected a slipped secret. Many major stories are picked up from unwitting remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment of Trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience provides reporters means to estimate the worth of information; liars may be nervous or overly glib, and knowledge of the person's past record is of great value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop ability to judge character and truthfulness; corroborate doubtful statements and use past record to assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Good, brief quotations put life into a story; reporters should watch for striking, characteristic, or significant phrases and get them exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations should be exact, but it's legitimate to correct faulty grammar so the subject appears to speak good English. Use quotes to break monotony and add human interest; take care to record them accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interviewee refuses to talk, a reporter may rely on inference but must proceed with extreme caution to avoid libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inference as dangerous; carefully check material obtained by inference and refer it to the city editor for final judgment before including it. A truthful account of what was said/done in response to questions is seldom actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must be able to remember exactly what was said when notebook use is impossible, but should not rely too much on memory and must check every fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition (repeat name and answers) to fix details in memory; ask a question again to confirm wording. Nevertheless, verify and recheck all facts before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must have courage and perseverance to face rebuffs and discourtesy, sticking to assignments until they obtain the necessary copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persevere politely through rebuffs; question everybody who knows anything about a story, verify all information, and check names and addresses. Persistence is often rewarded with hard-to-get stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Types of Persons to Be Interviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewees typically fall into four types: (1) knows news and will talk, (2) will talk but doesn't know news, (3) refuses to talk, (4) seeks free advertising (self-advertiser).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle each type appropriately: (1) gather material readily; (2) prepare deeply and suggest points to elicit info; (3) use ingenuity, leading yes/no questions, sympathy, cajolery, brusqueness or inference as last resort; (4) set time limits, tell them what information you need, and cut short irrelevant self-promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Right Expression To Use (diction guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid incorrect or inexact word choices; prefer precise synonyms and accepted forms (list of specific corrections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: use 'dealt' not 'administered' for a blow; distinguish 'claim' vs 'assert'; use 'complexioned' (not 'complected'); 'aware' rather than 'conscious' when appropriate; use 'upon' or 'on' instead of 'onto'; 'virtually' not 'practically'; 'waistcoat' rather than 'vest' (vulgarism); 'general' not 'universal' in some contexts; 'neighborhood' vs 'vicinity'; 'point of view' instead of 'standpoint'. Use precise diction to improve clarity and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should organize notes according to a definite plan before writing to achieve speed, accuracy, fairness, clearness, and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start organizing as soon as facts are gathered; group notes so you can write without pausing to study them. Delete trivial details, jot down important points in intended order; preliminary preparation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed in composition is as valuable as quickness in gathering news — organised notes enable faster, cleaner writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrange notes into logical order before writing; ten minutes of organization can save twenty minutes at the typewriter and reduce errors caused by searching jumbled notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized material prevents haphazard writing that misweights facts and leads to stories being heavily edited or discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary arrangement allows estimation of relative importance of facts and avoids overplaying/underplaying details. Careful organization reduces the likelihood of copy being cut by copy readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorganized notes increase the chance of mistakes during composition; concentrated attention during writing is necessary for accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize notes so you do not have to interrupt writing to hunt for facts; check important details before they go into the story to avoid libel and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid editorial bias, especially in controversy coverage, notes must be handled so both sides are apparent and can be presented fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly organized notes make it easier to present balanced coverage; disorganized notes may cause even conscientious reporters to omit important details and produce unfair stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: A story written from an orderly arrangement of parts is clear; the reporter must keep time and space relations perfectly clear for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present facts in the exact order you want readers to receive them; clever arrangement of phases can achieve desired effects of unity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization of material increases reader interest because well-arranged notes let the reporter keep attention on composition and craft an engaging narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With notes at a glance the writer can maintain focus on phrasing and emphasis that maximize interest; discard trivialities and highlight human or newsworthy elements.
